transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-21
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Noah (Redwood SE), Liam (Cobalt CTO), Priya (ML Eng), Jonas (Infra), Sofia (Product)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on per-token economics and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated and Private for Cobalt's assistant product. Discussed batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization levers, budget constraints (~$12k/mo target to start), latency SLOs, and next steps for a small benchmark/pilot.

Topics:
- Current stack & usage profile
- Cost targets and acceptable latency tradeoffs
- Batching/caching knobs and expected unit cost reductions
- Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private feasibility and procurement timeline
- Security/compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC)

Action items (also in metadata): see above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood inference, joining me is noah our se. how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Liam (Cobalt): good, thanks. excited to dig in, we've been evaluating a few options. key thing for us is cost per call - our product is chat-based, average 350 tokens in/out but spikes to 1k on heavy contexts.
[00:20] Noah (Redwood): great, that's helpful. just to orient, are you currently self-hosting models or using a managed API?
[00:27] Priya (Cobalt): currently using a managed API, mix of open-checkpoint instances and some hosted LLM. monthly spend is creeping up, and we're looking to get better predictable unit economics.
[00:36] Jonas (Cobalt): infra cares about VPC and key management, so private connectivity is on the table too.
[00:42] Maya: perfect. today we wanted to walk through how batching and KV/prefix caching reduce per-token cost, and what tradeoffs look like between hosted, dedicated/reserved capacity, and private deployments. also understand your budget target.
[00:55] Sofia (Cobalt): to be explicit, leadership wants a starter budget of about $12k/mo for inference and they'd like to see a pilot before committing to reserved capacity.
[01:05] Noah: that's reasonable. quick note, our hosted API works well for fast time-to-value, but if you want predictable unit costs at scale, Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) or Private (VPC/on-prem) lets you amortize fixed infra and get lower per-token pricing, especially with batching + quantization.
[01:20] Liam: can you give rough numbers? ballpark per-token on hosted vs dedicated?
[01:25] Noah: rough baseline — for hosted, depending on model size, we often see an effective cost around $0.0008 to $0.0015 per token for medium-size LMs with default single-request throughput. with batching and KV cache, you can reduce apparent unit cost by 2-4x for workloads with repetition and long contexts. Dedicated committed capacity can push unit economics down further — maybe to $0.0002-$0.0006/token for heavy steady workloads after amortization and quantization. these are examples, exact depends on model, quantize profile and token distribution.
[01:53] Priya: okay, so with our 350 tokens average, at $0.0006 that's about $0.21 per call, that scales to...
[02:00] Liam: if we do 100k calls that's $21k, so exceeds our pilot budget.
[02:07] Maya: right, and that's why batching and prefix caching matter — they reduce GPU cycles per token. two levers to consider: (1) batching: combine concurrent requests to increase amortization across attention compute; (2) KV/prefix caching: for assistant flows where certain prompt prefixes are repeated, reusing KV cache avoids re-computing the prefix.
[02:26] Noah: also quantization — lower precision kernels (4-bit/8-bit) can improve throughput and lower cost but might impact quality slightly. Redwood Optimize can help recommend quantization profiles by workload.
[02:36] Jonas: how often do you see real production workloads benefit from KV cache? ours has a lot of repeated system prompts and policy text.
[02:42] Noah: very common — when you have long static system messages or few-shot examples that repeat across calls, prefix caching can cut compute by 30-70% for the recurring portion. if your dynamic user content is small relative to the prefix it can be even better.
[02:54] Priya: our main pain is spikes during reporting windows, concurrent concurrency peaks. how does batching interact with latency SLOs?
[03:02] Maya: good question — batching can increase tail latency if you wait too long to accumulate requests. Redwood lets you configure batching policy: max batch size, max latency wait (e.g., 10-50 ms), and priority buckets. for strict 95th pct latency <300ms you tune batching to favor latency (smaller batch windows). for throughput/cost you increase batch window and size.
[03:24] Liam: what about fallback behavior if dedicated capacity is saturated? we can't have our product degrade badly.
[03:30] Noah: smart routing handles that — fallbacks to higher-cost hosted instances or degraded model variants, and you can configure burst capacity. Dedicated includes burst pool options. for mission-critical endpoints you can set automatic fallback to hosted API within the same region with config to preserve availability.
[03:46] Sofia: security — what about KMS, audit logs, SOC2? leadership requires SOC2 and customer-managed keys.
[03:53] Maya: Redwood Hosted is SOC2 compliant; for customer-managed keys and VPC we offer Private (VPC/on-prem). Dedicated also supports VPC peering and KMS integrations. we provide audit logs, RBAC and SSO/SAML integrations for enterprise.
[04:07] Jonas: do you support HSM?
[04:10] Noah: yes, HSM integrations available for Private deployments; for Dedicated we support KMS via cloud provider KMS, and you can chain to your HSM where needed.
[04:17] Priya: back to costs — can you walk through an example with caching + batching for our profile? we have 40% repeat prefixes, average total tokens 350, 10 RPS peak.
[04:28] Noah: rough calc — baseline compute tokens per call = 350. with 40% prefix reuse you only compute ~210 tokens on average. batching at 10 RPS with batch window tuned to 20ms might yield effective throughput where GPU attends to more tokens per GPU second — let's say you get a 1.8x improvement from batching. combined 40% cache + 1.8x batching could reduce GPU token cost by ~2.8x to 3x. so if hosted baseline $0.0009/token, effective becomes ~$0.00032/token, turning that $0.315/call into $0.112/call.
[05:04] Liam: that's promising. if we do pilot at 50k calls, that's ~ $5.6k which is inside our pilot budget.
[05:11] Maya: exactly — pilots are usually hosted with config to measure real cache hit rates and then we model Dedicated savings for committed scale.
[05:19] Priya: how do you measure cache hit rate in the pilot?
[05:22] Noah: runtime exposes token-level telemetry — prefix hit/miss, KV cache reuse metrics, per-request token count and GPU ms. Redwood Console has dashboards per-route showing hit rate and cost breakdown. we can supply a trial dataset to run with our small benchmark script.
[05:36] Jonas: procurement-wise, how long to get Dedicated up and running? we need procurement lead times to factor into budgets.
[05:42] Maya: Dedicated setup is usually 4-8 weeks from contract signature depending on region and capacity. Private on-prem can take longer (6-12 weeks) due to network and security reviews. Hosted pilot can start within days.
[05:55] Sofia: do you have size/commit tiers? what minimum commit is typical?
[06:00] Maya: yes, Dedicated has commitments by GPU-hour/month. minimum varies but typically enterprises commit to enough capacity to justify a reserved cluster — e.g., a few hundred thousand tokens/day steady. We'll tailor a proposal to your projected monthly tokens.
[06:13] Priya: can you also help quantify the impact of quantization on quality? we worry about hallucinations.
[06:19] Noah: Optimize runs evals on your prompt set to estimate quality delta across quantization profiles; often 8-bit safe, some 4-bit profiles need more validation. we tie regression alerts to prompt sets so you can detect quality regressions post-deploy.
[06:33] Liam: what's included in the hosted per-token price? inference compute only? any request overhead fees?
[06:39] Maya: hosted per-token includes compute and basic request handling. there are add-ons like extended observability retention, private-link, or compliance packs which are extra. for Dedicated and Private we price reserved infra plus a platform fee.
[06:51] Jonas: can you show a sample pricing table?
[06:54] Maya: yes i'll send the pricing sheet. it'll include example scenarios: low-volume hosted, pilot hosted with caching assumptions, committed dedicated with amortization and quantization assumptions.
[07:02] Priya: about benchmarking, can you provide a reproducible script? we want something we can run in our environment to validate latency and concurrency behaviors.
[07:09] Noah: yes i'll share a small benchmarking harness that hits your workload shape — 350 token median, 1k token spikes — with toggles for batching window and cache warmup.
[07:18] Liam: timeline — we'll need internal go/no-go by end of month. is that realistic?
[07:23] Maya: yes if we get sample traces and you confirm budget numbers, we can kick off a pilot next week and have results within 7 days.
[07:30] Sofia: procurement will ask about SLA for Dedicated. what do you offer?
[07:33] Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; details in the enterprise contract. Hosted has best-effort SLAs for free tiers, and premium SLAs for paid tiers.
[07:43] Priya: can you walk me through an example calculation you mentioned earlier for 100k calls?
[07:47] Noah: sure quick back-of-envelope: 100k calls * 350 tokens = 35M tokens baseline. at hosted $0.0009/token = $31.5k. with 40% prefix cache and 1.8x batching, effective tokens = 35M * (1 - 0.4) / 1.8 ≈ 11.67M tokens billed compute-equivalent -> cost ≈ $10.5k. that illustrates how caching/batching flips the economics.
[08:14] Liam: interesting — we need to validate the 40% prefix assumption. our analytics team can produce trace samples.
[08:20] Maya: great, that's an action item.
[08:22] Priya: one more question — how do you charge for streaming responses? our assistant streams token-by-token for UI snappiness.
[08:27] Noah: streaming billing is typically the same per-token but you may generate slightly more tokens due to role tokens or system messages; KV cache still helps since you avoid re-compute of prefix. network egress is separate if you're in Private with your own infra.
[08:40] Jonas: any hidden costs we should plan for? e.g., storage for caches, logging retention?
[08:45] Maya: minimal storage costs for caching, included for hosted; for Private you manage storage and may have storage/network costs. extended observability retention is an add-on.
[08:54] Sofia: let's talk objections — leadership worried about vendor lock-in if we go Dedicated or Private.
[08:59] Maya: understood — we provide model-agnostic runtimes and standard model formats; you can export model artifacts and configs. Dedicated and Private give you more control, and the rollout policies let you pin model versions so your stack isn't tied to a single hosted-only API.
[09:12] Liam: final question — after pilot, if we want to move to Dedicated, how do we project savings?
[09:17] Noah: we'll run the pilot, capture real token counts, cache hit rates, and latency distribution. then we model amortization on a dedicated cluster with expected utilization and quantization profile. we can deliver a modeled unit-cost and break-even timeline by comparing incremental CAPEX/commit vs hosted monthly spend.
[09:33] Maya: recap and next steps — i'll send pricing sheet and example scenarios, noah will send the benchmark harness and recommended batching/KV config, priya will share sample traces. we'll aim to have pilot kickoff early next week if budget ok.
[09:47] Liam: that works for us. thanks both.
[09:50] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and artifacts.

(occasional transcription noise: 'K-V cash' for KV cache, 'quantize' sometimes 'con-quantize')

End of transcript.
